C-HOM-001E.title_en: The Hexameter Workshop: Composing Live from a Stock of Ready-Made Parts
C-HOM-001E.title_zh: 六音步的构件库：用现成套语在表演中即时成篇
C-HOM-001E.description_en: The Homeric epics were sung to audiences at festivals and sacrifices, and the singer had to weave tens of thousands of hexameter lines live under performance pressure. What makes this possible is a stock of assemblable parts: fixed combinations such as swift-footed Achilles, rosy-fingered dawn and the kindly dark are kept ready by metrical position, so that one character has five or six finished phrases depending on where in the line he must fall. Above the phrase lie the type-scenes - arming, feasting, sacrifice, guest-reception - with their fixed skeletons of action, and above those lie themes such as the disguised wanderer's return. Composition is thus moved from inventing words to selecting and assembling them, leaving attention for the architecture and the audience. The requirements: the parts must lock together (any adjacent pair must scan and make sense), and variation is reserved for the one or two beats that decide the outcome - repetition here is not a flaw but a facility, since one phrase tells the listener who has entered and in what situation.

C-HOM-002E.title_en: Ring Composition: Making a Passage Close by Returning to Its Opening
C-HOM-002E.title_zh: 环形包孕：让段落的开头与结尾互相抱住
C-HOM-002E.description_en: Homer's audience heard the poem once, by ear, so long passages needed to be locatable and memorable. Ring composition answers this: a passage's opening is answered at its close by the same words, image or action, while the middle may travel far and even nest several layers deep. Iliad 1 is the fullest sample - it opens on the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon over the division of spoil and closes through the appeal to Thetis, her audience with Zeus, his promise to punish the Achaeans, and the quarrel of the gods, so insult, appeal and pledge form one closed circuit; the poem as a whole answers its opening wrath only in Book 24, with the return of Hector's body and the funeral. The device gives closure, memory handles and meaning, since an image returning at the end has been re-meaned by everything between. The requirements: the echo must be recognisable, the return must be altered by the middle, and the nesting must not exceed what an ear can track in one pass.

C-HOM-003E.title_en: The Extended Simile: Importing a Whole Second World into a Comparison
C-HOM-003E.title_zh: 长明喻：把整个第二世界搬进一句比较里
C-HOM-003E.description_en: The Homeric extended simile does not settle for a one-word analogy; it imports an entire scene. Two armies meet as a mountain torrent smashes two boulders together; a falling soldier is a poppy bowed by rain in a garden; Achilles hunts Hector as a falcon hunts a dove; the tears of Odysseus are snow melting into a river. The comparanda come almost entirely from the world of peace - farming, herding, hunting, carpentry, seafaring, seasons. The device suspends the present event, unfolds a small self-sufficient picture with its own agent and details, and returns at the sentence's end to the thing compared. Its effects are three: thickness, as the audience is carried into the world of ploughman and craftsman and the narrative shows a whole society; tempo, as a calm image inside violence creates a breath and prevents violence from being consumed as continuous stimulation; and judgement, since the second world carries its own evaluation - comparing a soldier to a felled tree says more than he died. The requirements: the picture must stand alone, must come from another domain, and the return must land on the point of likeness.

C-HOM-004E.title_en: In Medias Res and Embedded Narration: Starting Late, Handing the Past to a Character
C-HOM-004E.title_zh: 中段开场与内嵌叙述：从最晚处起讲，把过去交给当事人
C-HOM-004E.description_en: The Iliad does not begin with the outbreak of war but with the ninth year, the plague and the quarrel; the Odyssey does not begin with the fall of Troy but with the tenth year after it, the hero held on Calypso's island while his son is besieged by suitors at home - and the protagonist does not appear until Book 5. The missing past is supplied by two devices: the narrator's compressed retrospect and embedded narration, above all Odyssey 9-12, where Odysseus at the Phaeacian court tells in the first person of the Cyclops, Circe, the Sirens and the dead (the apologoi). The arrangement compresses ten years of wandering into what can be heard, hands the narrative right to the participant, turns his own account into a live examination of his character before hosts who are simultaneously audience and judges, and keeps an outside view alive so the telling can be checked against his conduct. The requirements: the entry point must already be high-tension, the retrospect cut to the minimum needed, and the first-person narration given an on-stage audience and a stated reason.

C-HOM-005E.title_en: Humanizing the Enemy: Giving the Other Side a Name and a Grief
C-HOM-005E.title_zh: 敌方人性化：让敌人成为可哭的人
C-HOM-005E.description_en: The Iliad is a war poem from the Greek side, and yet it gives its most moving passages to the Trojans. Book 6 has Hector return to the city to take leave of Andromache and the infant Astyanax: he foresees the sack and his wife's slavery, goes back to the wall anyway, and prays that his son will be better than he. Book 24 has his father Priam enter the enemy camp by night, take Achilles' knees and kiss the hands that killed his son, and weep with him - one for his own father and for Patroclus, the other for Hector - followed by a shared meal, a truce, the return of the body and a funeral. The mechanism: give the adversary a concrete name, family and intelligible motives; let him speak before his own people; write the other side's losses as named laments; stage one action crossing the line at the point of greatest enmity; and alternate killing with mourning. The requirements: the enemy must not be reduced to a target, nor stripped of his own choices and errors - the sympathy is a mirror, not an ornament.

C-HOM-006E.title_en: The Ledger of Honour: Reducing Conflict to Public Rules of Distribution
C-HOM-006E.title_zh: 荣誉账本：把冲突还原为公开的分配规则
C-HOM-006E.description_en: The subject of the Iliad is not anger but a distribution conflict. The allied army divides spoil by contribution, and Achilles holds the captive Briseis as the tangible mark of his share; to replace his own loss the commander Agamemnon takes that share by sheer authority, so Achilles withdraws, the Greeks are beaten, and only when Agamemnon admits publicly that he was blinded and delivers the promised list of gifts are the accounts actually adjusted. The transferable points: reduce the opposition to a public ledger of standards, shares, adjudicator and procedure for change; translate the humiliation into a measurable debit on that ledger; make the settlement a publicly verifiable adjustment witnessed by all rather than a private soothing; and acknowledge that asymmetric power makes advice fail - the lavish list of Book 9 is refused because it is still set unilaterally by the side that took the share, so the difference is not quantity but whether the procedure is public.

C-HOM-007E.title_en: Double Motivation: Holding Necessity and Choice True at Once
C-HOM-007E.title_zh: 双重动因：让必然与选择同时成立
C-HOM-007E.description_en: The epics say two apparently contradictory things at once: events are fated, and people decide for themselves. Achilles is told his death is fixed and also weighs in Book 9 the two destinies his mother gave him - stay before Troy for imperishable fame and an early death, or sail home for a long life and a fading name - and chooses. Zeus lifts the golden scales to weigh lives at the decisive moment while the characters still act from their own anger and judgement; Hector goes out to fight knowing the city will fall and his wife be enslaved. The double statement is deliberate, not muddled: the sentences about fate or divine will state that things could not end otherwise, the sentences about motive state how the agent arrived at that end. Its function is to keep both the solemnity and sense of limit that necessity brings and the responsibility and character that choice brings. The requirements: write both layers fully and keep them separate, give the choice a checkable logic of character, lay out the two roads explicitly at the decisive point, and never let one layer explain the other away.

C-HOM-008E.title_en: Guest-Friendship: Running One Reception Rule Through Every Host and Place
C-HOM-008E.title_zh: 待客之礼：用一套接待规则测试所有人与所有地点
C-HOM-008E.description_en: The structural spine of the Odyssey is a rule of guest-friendship: a stranger must be brought in, seated, bathed, fed, given gifts, housed and escorted, while the guest must behave, repay and not consume the host's property. Odysseus' journey home becomes a continuous test of that rule: the Cyclops eats his guests, the extreme violation; Circe detains hers by magic; the Phaeacians keep it fully and carry him home; the suitors abuse it for years in his own house; and the poorest host, the swineherd Eumaeus, receives a strange beggar as well as he can. The same test is run through every person and place, and each host's conduct delivers the verdict without narration. The requirements: the rule must be observable and reusable, the test applied unannounced so nobody performs for the examiner, and one contrast case kept who keeps the rule under the worst conditions, so that circumstance cannot be pleaded as an excuse for violation.

C-HOM-009E.title_en: Disguise and Staged Recognition: Confirming Identity at the Last Possible Moment
C-HOM-009E.title_zh: 伪装与分级认出：用标记物把身份确认推到极点
C-HOM-009E.description_en: The second half of the Odyssey is a book of recognitions. The returned Odysseus is turned into an old beggar by Athena, so identity is screened and the recognition broken into stages, granted only to those entitled to it. The old dog Argos knows his master first and dies at once, a recognition without words and without error. The old nurse Eurycleia finds the boar's-tusk scar on his thigh while washing his feet and is silenced at once, since recognition here is handled as a risk. The swineherd and cowherd are tested and then brought in; his son Telemachus is shown the truth; and his wife Penelope is kept for last, setting a trap with a secret sign only her husband could know - the bed carved from a living olive stump, which cannot be moved - and accepting him only when he passes it. The delay does three jobs: safety, since a leak destroys the plan; verification, since only those sharing the past may confirm; and feeling, since the whole separation compresses into the instant of acknowledgement. The requirements: order the layers by entitlement and risk, reserve the final proof for a non-imitable shared sign, and give every stretch of delay a task.

C-HOM-010E.title_en: Kleos Aphthiton: Delivering the Work as a Community's Memory Institution
C-HOM-010E.title_zh: 以诗存名：把作品当作共同体的记忆制度
C-HOM-010E.description_en: The epics state their own function in the first line: the poet asks the Muse for the song, the song is of the wrath that brought countless pains, and what the heroes fight for is imperishable glory, a name that does not rot with the body. The epic is therefore a memory institution: sung to a community at festivals and sacrifices, it fixes in recitable form the names of heroes, the genealogies of families, the origins of rites and the shared values. The poems are repeatedly conscious of this: Achilles chooses between two fates and takes the short life with the name; Sarpedon explains to his companion why men risk death for honour - we hold the best portions precisely because we stand in the front line; and the bard Demodocus sings heroic deeds while his audience weeps. The transferable points: decide what and why the community must remember, design a recitable, re-performable form that does not depend on the author's presence, write how one will be remembered into the internal value system, and keep losses and costs in the record, or transmission degrades into celebration or propaganda.
